lesson.title: Solid Evidence: Identifying Ions by Their Precipitates
lesson.summary: Precipitate identification reads the color, mass, and behavior of a solid formed in a precipitation reaction to pin down exactly which ions produced it.
lesson.body:
Once you know a precipitation reaction is predicted to occur, the next skill is reading the solid that actually forms: its color, its texture, and how it behaves under a few follow up tests, all of which narrow down exactly which ions were present. This builds directly on qualitative analysis, where a precipitate is treated as evidence, and on precipitation reactions, where the solubility rules tell you which ion combinations are expected to be insoluble in the first place.

Color is often the fastest clue. Silver chloride, AgCl, forms a curdy white precipitate that darkens on exposure to light. Lead iodide, PbI2, forms a striking bright yellow solid, sometimes called the golden rain reaction when it is precipitated slowly and allowed to crystallize. Barium sulfate, BaSO4, forms a fine white precipitate that is essentially insoluble even in acid, which is exactly why it is used medically as a contrast agent: it will not dissolve in stomach acid. Color alone, though, is not always enough, since several different white precipitates exist, so a second test is often needed to distinguish between them, such as checking solubility in dilute nitric acid or in ammonia.

Precipitate identification can also be done quantitatively, by comparing the measured mass of a precipitate to the mass predicted for different candidate ions. Suppose an unknown solution is known to contain 0.00500 mol of a divalent metal cation, M2+, and excess sodium sulfate solution is added. A white precipitate forms, is filtered, dried, and weighed, giving a mass of 1.167 g. Dividing mass by moles gives the molar mass of the precipitate: 1.167 g / 0.00500 mol = 233.4 g/mol. Comparing that to the molar masses of likely sulfate precipitates, barium sulfate, at 137.33 + 32.07 + 4 x 16.00 = 233.40 g/mol, matches almost exactly, while calcium sulfate, at 136.14 g/mol, and strontium sulfate, at 183.68 g/mol, do not. The precipitate's mass identifies the cation as Ba2+.

This result also makes physical sense given real solubility behavior. Barium sulfate is extremely insoluble, so essentially all of the barium present precipitates out and the measured mass reflects the true amount of metal in solution. Calcium sulfate, by contrast, is only moderately insoluble, so if the unknown had actually been Ca2+, a meaningful fraction would have stayed dissolved and the measured precipitate mass would have come out low, an important reminder that quantitative precipitate identification only works cleanly when the precipitate involved is genuinely close to insoluble.

Put together, precipitate identification uses three lines of evidence: color and texture as a first read, mass as a quantitative check against candidate compounds, and, when needed, an independent test like solubility in acid or a flame test to break any remaining tie. This same logic, generate a solid, then interrogate it, is the direct ancestor of the more rigorous volumetric methods that follow, where instead of weighing a solid you measure a volume of liquid with equal precision.
